comments.author: @BxKRs
comments.text: I miss my darkroom days.  Black and white processing involves projecting the image onto a paper with silver crystals for several seconds (all depends on the exposure of the film and any filters added to increase or decrease contrast) then submerging in a developer solution, followed by a stopper (literally stops developing) then a fixer which “fixes” the paper which prevents the page from continuing to react to light.  This process was done in low light, usually red.  The film development process must be done in complete darkness.  I can still smell the vinegary chemical smell, which I was quite fond of.

Personally, while I enjoy messing around with the free tiers of many of these ai, I am awaiting a day when we can run fully multimodal ai "beings" on a single device. Without it costing ten thousand dollars plus. 

I can run comfyui locally among other things, each as an individual instance. But any one of those overheats my power brick eventually. Not my GPU, just the power brick. 😅 maybe I'll upgrade that soon and see what I can do..

But I predict that some next gen consumer grade ai specific chips will make it possible to combine open source models into your own ai productivity companion. And I would argue, one that may likely become your best friend, or even more.

Until then though, I see no issue with using done middle man if it generates productivity or solves issues. For example, I am working on music videos and want to find a good video upscaler for some clips that I like but are too low quality.

This is such a mix. On one hand, yes AI will enable more people to create things and this slide deck presents some great ideas. But then - Companionship + Social? Holy shit is there some dystopian creepery in here. It's basically saying "Don't make REAL friends, have AI create some for you!" and the direct quote of "we expect to see messaging & social apps where bots are treated as equal citizens" - are they fucking crazy? 

IMO, this investment firm presents a very strong case for not seeking investors in the first place. Use AI to build things on your own outside your day job - or if you do need coworkers, start your idea with some people you trust and establish it as a worker's cooperative. Make sure the people who make the thing are the ones who reap the financial reward, not investors siphoning off the product of your labor. 

And for shit's sake, don't make "friendship as a service" your business model.

comments.author: @Role-Play_Gamer
comments.text:
It's funny when me as an artist is the one arguing with people who are not artists and hate AI art in "defense" of artists. Dedicated artists will be able to use AI to produce wayyyy more high quality content than any person who is just messing around for fun. Artistic skill isn't just stroking the canvas;  the artistic eye developed over years is also a learned skill. If AI can multiply artists' productivity by thousands of times, then those of us who have thousands of artist pieces we want to create won't feel overwhelmed by the impossibility of doing it all manually.

If people find the process of drawing fun, they can still do so after AI is better than them. If they draw just to make money, they can just adapt to new processes. If they just have the need to feel special through a scarcity if high quality art, then that is just an insecurity issue.

Creative AI is amazing for so many other reasons as well! When individuals are able to create games, language translations/localizations, movies, anime, or anything else, original or fan content from copyrighted IPs, we won't have to worry about the censorship and guidelines big companies abide by, or in the case of adaptations, completely butchering the IP. Video Game movies are one great example of that. They're definitely getting a lot better than they used to be, but they're still very far from perfect. The difference between fans and companies is that the fans actually care about accurate character personalities, designs, and lore.

comments.author: @seppimweb5925
comments.text: The video offers interesting insights into the role of AI in democratizing technologies and services. However, I find the use of the term 'luxury' in this context misleading. When I think of luxury, images of caviar, Ferraris, and private jets come to mind – things that clearly symbolize wealth and exclusivity. The accessibility of formerly specialized or advanced offerings to a wider audience through AI is undoubtedly valuable, but it should be referred to as 'democratization' or 'expansion of access' rather than luxury. It's not about traditional luxury here, but about providing value and opportunities to all layers of society. More precise language would help convey the actual benefits of these technological advances more accurately and avoid misunderstandings

comments.text:
how you put images from filmn into real paper?
well film is a negative of a true picture (flipped colors). So you put photosensitive paper under the negative film, then you use magnifing glass to zoom (make it bigger). in this step you also crop the image. Then you use lamp light to pass through negative film, mangnifing glass onto photosensitive paper to create an image there. Then you put into those papers into baths to protect photosensitive layer of paper from further exposure.
Red light is lowest energy light and don't influence the paper that much. 
I am not phototechnician - I saw it somwhere... my description might be off a bit :)
